title: The Moon Without a Flaw
eyes: Michitsuna's Mother (Fujiwara no Michitsuna no Haha)
Sugawara no Takasue's Daughter (author of the Sarashina Nikki)
places: Her own house in the capital, waiting on Kaneie's visits
Teishi's quarters in the palace and her temporary residences
Michinaga's Tsuchimikado mansion and the palace
The Tsuchimikado mansion and the inner palace, at the centre of every decision
At court ceremonies as a high-ranking participant
Constantly at the emperor's side in the palace
Her house in the capital, then Prince Atsumichi's palace
The eastern provinces and the Tōkaidō road, then a modest house in the capital
intro: Around the year 1000, a city of perhaps a hundred thousand people at the foot of the eastern hills held a court of a few thousand nobles, and its politics were made largely in women's rooms. An emperor's heir came from his consort's family, so the Fujiwara clan placed daughters at the emperor's side and waited for sons. Emperor Ichijō had two such wives. Empress Teishi was the daughter of Michitaka, whose branch fell from power in 995–96. Empress Shōshi was the daughter of his younger brother Michinaga, who outlasted everyone. Each empress drew a salon of gifted women around her, and those women wrote. Sei Shōnagon's Pillow Book remembers Teishi's court as a place of jokes, snow mountains and flutes, and it is strikingly silent about that court's disgrace. Murasaki Shikibu, recruited into Shōshi's household, wrote the Tale of Genji and a diary of the birth of Michinaga's grandson. In it she took an acid swipe at Sei Shōnagon, whom she may never have met. Izumi Shikibu's love diary shows what the gossip machine did to a woman without a faction behind her. Beside the women's kana diaries ran the men's. These were daily records in kanbun, a Japanese form of classical Chinese, kept so that precedent could be consulted later. Michinaga's own autograph diary is terse and practical and leaves out what mattered most to him. Sanesuke, his critical senior colleague, wrote down the boastful 'full moon' poem Michinaga himself did not record. Yukinari, the emperor's secretary, gives the most intimate account of Teishi's death, a day both great men's diaries pass over in silence. Setting these side by side shows the same few rooms through glances that do not agree. A birth that Murasaki records as terror, sweat and ruined make-up appears in her patron's diary as a list of rites. A banquet poem survives only because its hearer disapproved. A death goes unrecorded by the men who gained most from it. The chapter is framed by two outsiders. Michitsuna's Mother, wife of Michinaga's father, wrote the first woman's diary a generation earlier. Her niece, the Sarashina diarist, was born in the very year of the imperial birth and arrived in the capital in 1020 as a twelve-year-old who wanted nothing in life except to read Genji. By then Michinaga had his flawless moon, and the salons' rivalry had become literature.

title: Ash on the Wind
eyes: Vilém Slavata of Chlum and Košumberk
places: The family house and attic, Magdeburg, then the streets to the imperial camp east of the Elbe
Pillau, then the Pomeranian coast near Rügenwalde
intro: The Thirty Years' War began with a political gesture in Prague in May 1618, when Protestant Bohemian nobles threw two imperial governors and a secretary out of a castle window. It ended in October 1648 with two treaties negotiated at Münster and Osnabrück and signed at Münster. In the thirty years between, armies of Germans, Swedes, Spaniards, Croats, Scots, Walloons, Italians and Finns marched back and forth across central Europe. They were paid badly or not at all, and they fed themselves by taking food from farms and towns. Several million people died, more from hunger and plague than from fighting. Nobody living through it saw it as one war. A shoemaker near Ulm saw comets, inflation, plague and soldiers coming down the road again. A mercenary saw a list of quarters, sieges, paydays and burials. A nun in Bamberg saw her convent's gates and the colonel who might be persuaded to post a guard at them. A young Englishman in an ambassador's suite, riding to the Emperor in 1636, saw empty villages and dead people with grass in their mouths. This chapter sets those people side by side. The chapter centres on one day, 20 May 1631 by the Catholic calendar, when Tilly's and Pappenheim's imperial and Catholic League army stormed the Protestant city of Magdeburg on the Elbe. Within about twelve hours the city had burned, and roughly 20,000 people were dead. Five eyes meet there. Peter Hagendorf, a mercenary in Pappenheim's regiment, was shot twice at the Neustadt gate while his wife went into the burning streets to loot. Otto Guericke, a city councillor and engineer, lost everything and later wrote the most famous account. Zacharias Bandhauer, a Catholic canon whom the Protestant town had expelled, came back in with the victors. Daniel Friese was a boy of twelve. Pappenheim, the general, wrote a letter counting the dead and the soldiers' new wealth. Around that centre are quieter eyes. Hans Heberle, a cobbler-farmer in Ulm territory, kept a 'Zeytregister' (time-register) from the 1618 comet to old age. He fled with his family again and again, buried most of his children, and gave thanks for the peace in 1648. Johannes Junius, mayor of Bamberg, wrote to his daughter from a witch-trial prison in 1628. His other daughter, Maria Anna, a Dominican nun, later chronicled the Swedish occupation of the same city. Anna Wolff, a miller's daughter in Schwabach, hid in a dovecote for five days. An unnamed villager at Gerstetten wrote in his family Bible in 1647 about resettling empty cottages. Read together, these accounts show the war as an economy and a climate as much as a series of battles. The soldier and the farmer were connected by plunder. The nun's convent depended on a colonel's mood. One city's ash fell on villages miles away. The peace arrived as news, a church service and a discharge from service. These were not people who saw history from a height. Their writing shows ordinary life slowly giving way.

title: The Bills, the Bonfire and the Fire
eyes: Willem van de Velde the Elder
C. Groenveld, Pieter IJsbrand van der Hof and C.G. Kleyn (Hoorn verse writers)
places: a household outside the City walls
an alley near his home, City
Kent Street, Southwark, to St James's
with the Dutch fleet, southern North Sea
with the Dutch fleet off the Thames estuary
the Vlie, between Vlieland and Terschelling
Seething Lane; the Tower; Whitehall; Bankside
Gracechurch Street, Cornhill, the Royal Exchange
Barking church steeple; Moorfields; the Exchange
intro: In the summer of 1665 London began to die by the printed page. Every Thursday the parish clerks' Bills of Mortality reported the week's burials, and across England people copied the numbers: 112, then 1,089, then over 6,000 of plague alone in a week. The court fled to Salisbury and Oxford; the rich followed in coaches. Those who stayed — officials, clergy, the poor — lived among red crosses on doors, dead-carts and empty streets. Perhaps a hundred thousand Londoners, nearly a quarter of the city, died in eighteen months. All the while England was at war with the Dutch Republic, its great rival for trade. The plague did not stop the Second Anglo-Dutch War: thousands of Dutch prisoners filled Kent castles, the fleets fought the Four Days' Battle in June 1666 and the St James's Day Battle in July, and in August an English squadron under Robert Holmes burned well over a hundred Dutch merchant ships in the Vlie and the town of West-Terschelling. London lit bonfires to celebrate. Three weeks later the bonfire was London. In the small hours of Sunday 2 September 1666 a fire in Thomas Farriner's bakery in Pudding Lane, fanned by an east wind after a dry summer, ran down to the river and across the timber city. By the time it was stopped on the 5th and 6th it had destroyed some 13,200 houses, 87 parish churches, the Royal Exchange, Guildhall and St Paul's. Rumours that the French or Dutch had started it led mobs to attack foreigners; a confused French watchmaker, Robert Hubert, was hanged for it though he had not even reached London until the fire was two days old. These eyes stand at every distance from the disaster. Pepys and Evelyn were royal officials inside or beside the city; Vincent and Allin were dissenting ministers who stayed to preach and heal; Taswell was a schoolboy in the crowd. Josselin, a vicar in Essex, met it all as copied numbers and fast days. Far to the north, the rector of Eyam, William Mompesson, wrote letters from a village that had sealed itself in with the plague. Across the sea, the Dutch draughtsman Willem van de Velde sketched the battles from the enemy fleet, and a Venetian ambassador in Paris heard how England's rivals read its ruin. Read together, they show how one catastrophe looked different from every angle: a ledger of figures, a judgement of God, a chance for profit, a strategic windfall, a personal grief. Notice how often they rhyme — the same bill of mortality copied in London and Essex, the Vlie bonfire and the London fire paired in Paris, and the day a rector in Derbyshire wrote farewell letters just as a baker's oven in London was banked for the night. One famous source is missing on purpose: Daniel Defoe's A Journal of the Plague Year (1722) is a novel, written by a man who was about five in 1665. It is brilliant and well-researched, but it is fiction, and it is not one of the eyes here.

title: Rien: The Revolution Seen from Every Window
eyes: Anonymous planter of the Northern Province
places: Versailles, a window at Mme de Flahaut's
on the road in Lorraine, walking a hill
Châtillon woods near Meudon, then Versailles
her lodgings in the Marais, Paris
Versailles, then the Tuileries, then the Temple prison
his shop and the streets around rue Saint-Jacques, Paris
Paris in June and early July 1789, then the roads of Lorraine, Alsace and Franche-Comté
intro: On 14 July 1789 the king of France wrote one word in his journal, and it was 'nothing'. The word meant only that he had not hunted. That gap between the page and the street is the theme of this chapter. The Revolution was made in the gaps: between Versailles and Paris, between rumour and event, and between what a visitor felt in May and what he wrote in September. The first cluster is July 1789. Arthur Young, who had listened to the Palais-Royal orators in June, rides east and watches Strasbourg's town hall gutted. The Paris bookseller Hardy logs alarm bells and heads on pikes as reports reach his shop. A Norwich doctor, Edward Rigby, sees the heads of de Launay and Flesselles go by. On the 22nd Gouverneur Morris is waiting for his carriage when Foulon's head arrives. The same evening Jefferson sends Madison an account of a victory, with the killing in a postscript. Then the royal family's own pages: Louis's flat log of 5 and 6 October 1789 and of Varennes, his sister Élisabeth's sharp letters, and his daughter's later memoir of disguises, the reporters' box on 10 August 1792, and the last supper in the Temple. Against them stand Rosalie Jullien, a republican mother cheering the guns of 10 August, and Restif de la Bretonne, roaming the September nights with a novelist's licence. The execution of 21 January 1793 is seen at close range by the valet Cléry and the confessor Edgeworth, both writing later and both royalists. The best-placed foreign diarist in Paris, Morris, kept a diary from March 1789 to 1816, and it breaks off on 5 January 1793. It resumes only after he left Paris in October 1794. That silence is itself evidence of what keeping a diary under the Terror could cost. The English radicals close the chapter. Helen Maria Williams fell in love with the Revolution at the Federation of 1790 and met it again from inside a prison. Mary Wollstonecraft watched the king ride to his trial and found herself in tears. The queen's last letter, never delivered, is the last page written inside the Terror; Morris's retrospect from Hamburg closes the file. Read together, these eyes do not agree, and they are not meant to. They show how a revolution looks from the throne, the shop counter, the salon window, the roads of the provinces and the scaffold.

title: The Road to Moscow and Back
eyes: Christian Wilhelm von Faber du Faur
places: Kirgaliczky, near Suderva (Lithuania), on the road beyond Vilna
Beshenkovichi (Biešankovičy), on the Dvina, at the Khreptovich manor
In woods about 60 leagues from Moscow
Near Gzhatsk, on the Moscow road
Borodino, with III Corps before the Bagration flèches and Semenovskoye
Dressing stations behind the French centre, Borodino
With the Semenovsky Guards in the Russian reserve, Borodino
Russian headquarters, Borodino, then on the Mozhaisk road
Kremlin, escaping through a postern toward the Petrovsky Palace
Voronovo, his country estate near Tarutino
Between Braunsberg and Elbing, East Prussia
intro: On 24 June 1812 the largest army Europe had yet seen began crossing the Niemen into the Russian Empire. It was French only at its core. Germans from Hesse, Württemberg and Bavaria, Italians, Poles, Swiss, Croats and Portuguese marched with it. Six months later a few tens of thousands of frostbitten men came back over the same river. In between came the summer marches through Lithuania, the burning of Smolensk, the slaughter at Borodino, five weeks in a Moscow that burned around them, and a retreat that became one of the great disasters in military history. This chapter lines up the people who wrote it down while it was happening, or tried to. A Hessian captain records the hours his company stood under Russian guns and the coffee he took from his dead cook's pocket. Two soldier-artists, a Württemberger and a Bavarian, date their sketches by place and day, so their portfolios read as visual diaries. A bored commissary who would become Stendhal writes to his sister and his friends about lost breeches and lost manuscripts. Napoleon's surgeon writes to his wife from Moscow. Napoleon himself writes to Paris about wine cellars, then about blowing up the Kremlin. On the other side stand Kutuzov, who called Borodino a victory and then gave up Moscow, and Rostopchin, Moscow's governor, who promised to defend the city, then emptied it and may have set it alight. A nineteen-year-old Guards lieutenant writes and draws his war. A British general at Russian headquarters fumes that the French are being allowed to escape. Inside the occupied city, a French actress and a Russian deacon's wife are left to survive among the looters; both told their stories only years later. Far away, in the capital Napoleon never reached, the American minister John Quincy Adams reads the bulletins and the rumours and tries to work out the truth. On 15 September, the day Napoleon moved into the Kremlin, his baby daughter died. The scale of the two events could hardly be more different, but they share a date. These eyes do not agree. The commander's dispatch, the memoirist's set piece and the captain's pencilled hours describe the same days in different worlds. Where entries cluster, at Borodino, in the week of the fire, at Krasnoi, at the Berezina and on the frozen road to Vilna, the reader can watch the gap open between what headquarters believed and what the ranks endured.

title: A House Divided, Written Down
places: LeConte house, South Carolina College, Columbia
Washington, Seward's house and the Petersen house
St. Helena Island and Camp Saxton, Port Royal, South Carolina
Camp Saxton, Smith plantation, near Beaufort SC
Camp Saxton and the regiment's camps on the Sea Islands
Washington: White House, Navy Department, the Petersen house
LeConte house on the South Carolina College campus
intro: Four years, three quarters of a million dead, and four million people freed from slavery: the American Civil War was fought by a highly literate population that wrote constantly. Soldiers carried pocket diaries, planters' daughters kept journals under their beds, and cabinet secretaries wrote at midnight. Rarely has a war been recorded so densely from so many sides at once. This chapter gathers those records at five moments. At Fort Sumter in April 1861 the war began, watched from a Charleston rooftop and read about under the lamps of Broadway. On 1 January 1863 the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, and at Camp Saxton in South Carolina formerly enslaved soldiers, a free Black teacher and an abolitionist colonel recorded the same ceremony from yards apart. In July 1863 came Gettysburg and Vicksburg, seen by a British guardsman up a tree, a Rhode Island lieutenant in the line, a poet in the hospitals and the clerks of two capitals. On 17 February 1865 Columbia burned around a seventeen-year-old diarist, and on 14–15 April 1865 Lincoln died, with the Navy Secretary at the bedside and the news then spreading across the country. The eyes do not agree, and that is the point. Chesnut and Stone write the Confederacy's grief and, in Stone's case, open joy at Lincoln's death. Forten and Taylor record freedom as something lived, not granted. Fremantle came as an admiring foreign visitor and saw a defeat he did not fully grasp. Handy, a hostile witness, preserves the scale of a Black celebration that the law said should not have happened. Honesty about form matters here more than in most wars, because many famous 'diaries' were rewritten. Chesnut reworked hers in the 1880s, Whitman built Specimen Days from notebooks two decades later, and Susie King Taylor wrote her memoir in 1902. These are flagged and kept, because without them the Black and Confederate women's voices would thin out. Wherever a date or detail could not be re-verified for this edition, the entry is marked approximate.

title: Swimming in the Afternoon
places: Between Basseville and St Yvon, near Warneton
Moulin Rouge trench, Thélus / Neuville-Saint-Vaast, Artois
Transport Itonus, Lemnos to Anzac Cove
On the move with the Russian retreat, Galicia
Brandenburg Gate to the Reichstag, Berlin
intro: On 1 August 1914 a Tsar came home from evening prayers to learn that Germany had declared war on him; the next day a Prague insurance clerk wrote the same news in his diary and added that he went swimming. Those two entries, one dutiful and one notoriously flat, open a war that would eventually reach every continent and leave around ten million soldiers dead. This chapter does not try to tell that whole story. It sets a small number of real diaries and notebooks next to each other so that the reader can watch the same weeks arrive in very different rooms. The eyes are deliberately mixed. There are front-line men from four armies: a Saxon schoolteacher-lieutenant and an English quartermaster-sergeant on Christmas Eve 1914; a socialist barrelmaker from the Aude standing in a flooded trench in December 1915; a 21-year-old Ottoman lieutenant on the ridge the Australians called Lone Pine; a Rajput aristocrat serving as an aide in Flanders; an English poet watching the first morning of the Somme through binoculars. There are also people far behind the guns: a Berlin artist waiting for letters from her eighteen-year-old son, an Oxford student who learned of her fiancé's death by telephone in a Brighton hotel, an Arab clerk in wartime Jerusalem, an Australian war correspondent, and a cosmopolitan German count who walked through Berlin while the monarchy collapsed. The heart of the chapter is Gallipoli in the autumn of 1915. Lieutenant Mehmed Fasih's diary, kept in the trenches facing Anzac from mid-October, can be read day against day with the diary of the Australian correspondent Charles Bean and with ordinary Australian soldiers whose notebooks are now digitised by the State Library of New South Wales. The two sides are a few dozen metres apart, shelling, mining and freezing in the same November storm, and each describes the other almost entirely as noise: grenades, a machine gun on the slope, a mine going up on the right. Other clusters are thinner, and the chapter says so. The Christmas truce of 1914 is seen from both sides of the wire near Ploegsteert and Messines. December 1915 has a remarkable run: a French–German fraternisation in the mud on the 10th, a German company knocking over a British Christmas tree on the 25th, and a young woman in Sussex writing about a death on the 23rd. The first day of the Somme and the Armistice rest mostly on single voices here (Sassoon on 1 July 1916; Kessler in Berlin in November 1918), because the verification budget for this chapter ran out before more could be pinned down safely. Read side by side, the diaries show how little any one person knew. Kafka's war is a mood; the Tsar's is a sequence of meetings; Kollwitz's is a returned envelope; Fasih's is a list of the men he has lost; Kessler's revolution is quieter than the newspapers, and he notes that the trams and the water kept running.

title: Two Calendars, One Collapse
eyes: Dowager Empress Maria Feodorovna (Dagmar of Denmark)
places: Nevsky Prospekt and the Embassy, Petrograd
Nevsky Prospekt and a near-empty concert hall
Liteiny district and the Embassy, Petrograd
Imperial train, en route from Mogilev
Her flat near the Tauride Palace, Petrograd
Mariinsky Palace, Winter Palace, Smolny and Nevsky Prospekt, Petrograd
Morskaya and St Isaac's Square, Petrograd
Peter and Paul Fortress (Trubetskoy Bastion), Petrograd
Stavka at Mogilev and the imperial train at Pskov
Kiev, then the station and Headquarters at Mogilev
intro: In the last week of February 1917 by the Russian calendar — the second week of March by everyone else's — women queuing for bread in Petrograd started a strike, the strike turned into a march, and the soldiers sent to stop it joined in. Within eight days the Romanov dynasty, which had ruled for three centuries, was gone. Eight months later a second revolution put the Bolsheviks in the Winter Palace. Eight months after that, the former Tsar, his wife and their five children were shot in a cellar in the Urals. This chapter lines up people who wrote on the days themselves, or close to them. At the centre is Nicholas II, who kept his laconic diary through abdication and captivity, beside his wife Alexandra and his mother. Around them stand the Swiss tutor Pierre Gilliard, who went into captivity with them; the French ambassador Maurice Paléologue in the streets; the British ambassador's daughter Meriel Buchanan behind the embassy windows; and two American radicals, John Reed and Louise Bryant, notebooks open at Smolny. Then come the Russian writers, who took the revolution as a spiritual event. Zinaida Gippius was drunk on freedom in March and choking in November. Alexander Blok listened for the 'music' of revolution and wrote 'The Twelve'. Ivan Bunin in Moscow kept a diary of rage he would publish only in exile. The sociologist Pitirim Sorokin, a moderate socialist, went from Kerensky's office to a Bolshevik prison cell. Read side by side, they disagree about almost everything, including what day it is. On the night the Winter Palace fell Reed watched the ministers led out, while in the morning Gippius wrote of suffocation. The same week, in Siberia, the man who used to rule them all was clearing snow and complaining that the telegrams had stopped. The Tsar learned of October about a week late, from a provincial paper printed on packing paper. Several sources here are not pure diaries. Paléologue's journal was polished for publication, Gilliard's memoir quotes his own diary, and Reed's book is reportage built from dated notes. Each eye is labelled honestly, and wherever a day could not be confirmed the entry is marked approximate rather than given a false precision.

title: The Gate at Ginling
eyes: Soldiers of the 65th Infantry Regiment (Yamada Detachment), diaries compiled by Ono Kenji
Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shimbun / Osaka Mainichi Shimbun (war correspondents Asami Kazuo, Suzuki Jirō and others)
places: Ginling College campus, inside the Safety Zone
Mufushan, on the Yangtze north of the city
University Hospital and University Middle School
His house and compound on Xiaofenqiao, inside the Safety Zone, sheltering about 600 refugees
University Hospital, inside the Safety Zone
University of Nanking campus, inside the Safety Zone
Moving through the Zone and hospital with a 16 mm camera
Approaching and entering Nanjing from the east
Field headquarters near Suzhou, then Nanjing for the entry ceremony
North of the city along the Yangtze, at Mufushan
With his platoon in and around Nanjing
intro: In the autumn of 1937 the Japanese army fought its way up the Yangtze from Shanghai toward Nanjing, the capital of Nationalist China. The government left. Most foreigners left. A small group of about twenty Americans and Europeans, among them missionaries, teachers, doctors and a German businessman, stayed behind with Chinese colleagues. Late in November they set up a 'Safety Zone' of about four square kilometres in the western part of the city, hoping both armies would leave it alone. The city fell on 13 December. For the next six weeks or more, Japanese soldiers killed, looted, burned and raped across the city and the surrounding countryside, on a scale that the people inside the Zone could only partly measure. This chapter leaves out graphic detail on purpose. Its subject is what the diarists themselves wrote down: the size of what they saw, their fear, the long days at gates and in hospital wards, the arguments over food and flags and registration, and how they judged themselves. Minnie Vautrin, an American, and Cheng Ruifang, a Chinese dormitory matron, kept separate diaries at the same women's college on the same nights. They give us two views of one gate. John Rabe was a Siemens manager and a member of the Nazi Party. He used his swastika armband to turn soldiers out of his garden, and wrote to Hitler hoping he would help. The surgeons, professors and clergy around him wrote letters that went out in pieces, by gunboat or sewn into coat linings. Japanese records sit on the other side of the same days, and they are harder to read. A divisional commander noted the policy toward prisoners in his diary on the day the city fell. The theatre commander rode in at the head of a victory parade and wrote in his field diary. Rank-and-file soldiers of the 65th Infantry Regiment recorded the mass killing of prisoners near Mufushan, in diaries a factory worker named Ono Kenji gathered decades later. Back home, newspaper readers followed a 'contest' between two lieutenants that was reported like a sports score. It was printed as journalism, not kept as a diary, and it shows what Japanese readers were being told while the Zone's foreigners were writing protest letters. Many of these documents had to be fought over afterwards. Rabe's diary was not made public until December 1996. Matsui's diary was published in 1985 in an edition that critics found had been altered. Azuma Shirō's published diary led to a libel suit he lost at Japan's Supreme Court. Questions about how authentic the sources are, and how they should be read, belong to this event's history. Each entry below says how far it can be trusted. When these diaries are set side by side, the same week comes out very differently in each. To one writer it was a paperwork problem, to another a triumph, and to a third an emergency of the conscience. title: Only Tanya Is Left
places: Dresden, the Elbe meadows and burning old town
Berlin, borrowed attic flat and cellar
Basement of the Borochov school, 68 Nowolipki Street, Warsaw ghetto
Stalingrad, with the 308th Rifle Division (Gurtiev) near the silicate works
Site of Treblinka, east of Warsaw
Dresden, from 1940 in a 'Jews' House' with his non-Jewish wife Eva
Laubach, Hesse, a small town under local SS surveillance
9 Ilkley Road, Barrow-in-Furness, a shipbuilding town
Leningrad, living with her adoptive mother 'Mama' and the old family friend Aka
intro: On 1 September 1939 at least four people in this chapter opened a notebook or turned to a fresh page. A German court official in a small Hessian town began a secret diary that day because he wanted his grandchildren to understand how a democracy turns into a dictatorship. A fifteen-year-old Jewish schoolboy in Łódź went to bed half-dressed in case the sirens came. A young mother in Stockholm, not yet the author of Pippi Longstocking, bought tea, cocoa and soap and wrote that nobody could believe it. In London a Member of Parliament sat in the Commons and watched a Prime Minister fail to set a deadline. Six years later most of the Jewish diarists in this chapter were dead, and the people who survived were writing about cellars, rations and a surrender signed at Reims. This chapter does not try to cover the whole war. It sets a small number of real diaries next to each other so that their dates line up: the outbreak in September 1939; the fall of France in 1940; the invasion of the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941; the Leningrad hunger winter of 1941–42; the deportations of 1942–43 from Paris, Amsterdam, Łódź and Bucharest; D-Day on 6 June 1944; the Dresden raid of 13–14 February 1945; and the fall of Berlin and VE Day in April–May 1945. The Holocaust runs through the whole chapter, and these entries treat it with care. Dawid Sierakowiak, Hélène Berr, Etty Hillesum and Anne Frank did not survive. Victor Klemperer survived partly because of his marriage, and partly because the raid that destroyed Dresden on 13–14 February 1945, three days before he was due to report for deportation, let him remove his star and disappear among the homeless. Mihail Sebastian survived Antonescu's Romania and was killed by a truck three weeks after VE Day. Their entries are written as paraphrase in their own order of knowing: what they heard, what they guessed, and what they could not yet believe. Other vantages sit alongside them: a German anti-Nazi official recording a soldier's eyewitness account of mass shootings in 1941; two Leningrad girls whose notebooks both record 28 December 1941; a Berlin society journalist; an anonymous Berlin woman, now generally identified as Marta Hillers, writing in a cellar while the Red Army arrived; a Norwegian prisoner; a Swedish letter censor; and, handled carefully, the dictated diary of the Nazi Propaganda Minister, whose last entry is a bare military report. The vantage scale runs from the victims themselves to those who heard the news from a neutral capital. Several of these texts were revised by their authors, edited by relatives or reconstructed by archivists. Each eye's authenticity note says how, and the entries give the confidence of every date.

title: Under the Scorching Sun
places: Ryōgoku, Asakusa, Honjo and Suzaki, Tokyo
Aboard the Enola Gay, Tinian to Hiroshima and back
Home near the Communications Hospital, Hiroshima, about 1.5 km from the hypocentre
Tokyo Medical College evacuation site, Nagano Prefecture
Budget Committee room, National Diet Building
A hotel outside Tokyo, then the train to Tokyo
Police headquarters air-defence basement, then the burning Kōtō district
intro: In the last eight months of the Pacific War, a remarkable number of people on both sides kept private records they were in no position to publish. Tokyo novelists hid diaries that would have cost them their freedom. A police photographer wrote up his night in the firestorm before he went out to photograph the dead. A Filipino diplomat serving Japan's client republic set down the explosions outside his window. On the other side of the Pacific, a president, his secretary of war and his commerce secretary each wrote a few lines at night about a weapon most of the world had never heard of. A young co-pilot on Tinian filled a notebook during the flight that used it. This chapter places those voices side by side. The firebombing of Tokyo on the night of 9–10 March 1945 is seen by Ishikawa Kōyō, the Metropolitan Police photographer who nearly died in it, and by Uchida Hyakken, who watched refugees walk past in whatever they had on. Nagai Kafū lost his house and library that night. The medical student Yamada Fūtarō answered it with a cry for vengeance, and Leon Ma. Guerrero was woken by bombs just after midnight. Eleven weeks later, on 25–26 May, the raids came back for the rest of the city. Uchida, Yamada and the Diet's chief secretary Oki Misao were all burned out or fighting fires within the same few hours. Then the eye moves outward. At Potsdam on 24–25 July, Henry Stimson pressed Truman again to spare Kyoto. Truman wrote that the bomb would hit only military objectives, never women and children. A fortnight later, Robert Lewis logged the release over Hiroshima, and less than a mile from the blast centre Dr. Hachiya Michihiko was stripped of his clothes and burned. The record for Nagasaki is thinner, and this chapter says so. The account used here was written ten years later by a pathologist who was not in the city. Henry Wallace's diary of 10 August records Truman stopping further atomic bombing. On 15 August the eyes converge again, scattered now across a defeated country. In Kamakura, Takami Jun and Ōsaragi Jirō each heard the Emperor's broadcast under a blazing sun. In Okayama Prefecture, Tanizaki Jun'ichirō could not make out the radio and learned of the surrender from his weeping family. His refugee guest Kafū heard the news after a train ride and drank wine that evening to celebrate. In the mountains of Nagano, Yamada at first refused to believe it and then wept. What these voices share is the gap between what each could see and what was happening. Kiyosawa Kiyoshi was sure defeat would bring violence. He died of pneumonia in May, three months before he could test that belief. Truman believed his target was purely military. Yamada vowed revenge and ended the year still not believing everything he was told. No verified diary for the surrender ceremony on 2 September is included here. That gap is left open rather than filled with memory.

title: The Long Threads
eyes: Abu 'Ali al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Banna'
A Journal of the Plague Year: An Archive of COVID-19
places: Old Market Street, Sligo, then Ballyshannon
Sackville Street, a few streets from Broad Street, Soho
Washington, D.C., and Camp Humphreys, Virginia
Cape Town, on the voyage home
intro: Every other chapter in this book holds one event still and walks around it. This one moves through time instead. It follows a single recurring human experience, the epidemic arriving in an ordinary person's city, through the private notebooks of people who were not doctors or rulers but just kept writing while the death-carts went by. The thread starts earlier than most readers expect. In 1068–69 a Baghdad scholar, Abu 'Ali ibn al-Banna', kept a hurried autograph diary of births, deaths, quarrels, prices and rumours, and part of it survives. It shows that the daily private record is old and global, not a European invention. It also shows that a diarist's first instinct is the same in every century: write down the news, write down who died, write down what frightened you. Six centuries later Samuel Pepys watches red crosses appear on London doors and buys tobacco to chew against the infection. Two centuries after him, in New York in 1832, the ex-mayor Philip Hone watches cholera creep south from Quebec and calls his own city filthier than the places already struck. A merchant, George W. Strong, writes that he will take his family out of town. His son George Templeton Strong, by 1849 a young lawyer with a diary of his own, predicts the new wave will not be as bad as '32. In the west of Ireland Charlotte Stoker lives through Sligo's cholera summer and later writes it down for her son, Bram. In Soho in 1854 the physician John Snow dates, in a published letter, the evening he took his case against the Broad Street pump to the parish guardians. In the autumn of 1918 the thread runs through many hands at once. A Massachusetts mother's diary turns overnight into a list of the sick. A Vermont man records his own fever, then counts the town's dead ward by ward. A young Native American volunteer nurse writes from an army camp ward near Washington, and an Australian medical sergeant sketches Table Bay and notes how Cape Town collected its dead by lorry. In Vienna, Egon Schiele draws his dying wife and dies himself three days later. Then the thread changes its nature. Diarists stop being only private individuals and become contributors to institutions built to receive them. Mass Observation (Britain, 1937) asked ordinary people to write down a single day, 12 May, and in 2020 it asked them again, in lockdown. Archives in Pieve Santo Stefano, Emmendingen, London and an online project in Russia began collecting the notebooks that families used to burn. When COVID-19 arrived, archivists opened collecting projects within weeks, in some cases taking their name from the plague-year literature this chapter begins with. Read the eyes in this chapter as a relay rather than a crowd. Each one writes from inside a city waiting for news, counting the weekly dead, deciding whether to flee, and getting something wrong. The institutions at the end are the reason the next diarist's notebook may survive.
